Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:20: Also in the Tikkunim (59b) — see there — they explained several particulars regarding the matter of robbery. From there we learn the matter of repentance applying even in commandments, even in the precision of the commandments — such as whether one engaged in Torah properly or not. In this manner the discerning reader may infer to all matters in which some blemish applies, that repentance is needed, and one is called a "ba'al teshuvah" — for since the supernal grades are corrupted through his sin, and he restores the waters to their place, it is fitting that he be called a "ba'al teshuvah."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:21: They said there, of blessed memory: further, the commandment [against] "the plunder of the poor is in your houses" (Isaiah 3:14) — this is the Shechinah, for whoever robs prayer, which is charity [tzedakah] to the Righteous One, Life of the worlds, in whom eighteen blessings are included, is as though he robbed him of his own life, which is the Shechinah, of whom it is said (Ecclesiastes 9:9), "see life with the wife whom you love." So too, whoever detracts from the delight of Shabbat is as though he robbed his Shechinah, who is Shabbat, the only daughter — and this caused her to be robbed from him in exile, this being what is written (Isaiah 50:1), "and because of your transgressions your mother was sent away." And what is repentance? (Leviticus 5:23), "and he shall restore the stolen thing that he stole" — that he restore the Shechinah to her place. "Or the oppressed thing that he oppressed" — this is the Holy One, blessed be He, from whom she is separated — for the Shechinah is called "positive commandments" from the side of the right, and "negative commandments" from the side of the left, and Torah is called from the side of the central column; and whoever robs or oppresses regarding Torah and positive and negative commandments is as though he robbed the Shechinah from the arms of the Holy One, blessed be He. Likewise, from the side of Yesod, Life of the worlds, is called "commandments" — the commandment of circumcision; whoever robs in the covenant and brings his seed out into a foreign domain is as though he brought it out from a private domain into a public domain, causing the Shechinah to go out from her place, which is the Land of Israel, which is a private domain, and exiled her among the nations of the world, who are a public domain — this being what is written, "and because of your transgressions your mother was sent away." Therefore (Exodus 20:7), "you shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain" — what is "the name of your God"? This is the Shechinah; "in vain" — this is idolatry, to which she was exiled. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:22: Here it is proven from the passage that one who is obligated in a matter and does not perform it is called a robber, as it says, one who robs regarding Torah and positive commandments — and this is like the matter of withholding a hired worker's wage, which resembles theft.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:23: So too it is explained in Midrash Rabbah, parashat Bamidbar, in these words: another interpretation, "do not cut off," etc. (Numbers 4:18) — this is what is written (Proverbs 22:22), "do not rob the poor, for he is poor." Our sages said, of what does the verse speak? If he is poor, of what does he rob him? Rather, it speaks only of the gifts to the poor that one is obligated to give them from the Torah — gleanings, forgotten sheaves, the corner of the field, and the tithe for the poor — and the Holy One, blessed be He, warned that a person should not rob them of the gifts fitting to give them; "for he is poor" — his poverty suffices for him; it does not suffice that the wealthy man stands in ease while the poor man is in distress, but he even robs from him what the Holy One, blessed be He, gave him. — end of quotation. Similarly, this applies correctly to the matter of robbing Torah and commandments, as explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:24: Now, through the Rashbi's, peace be upon him, explanation of this verse regarding "and he shall restore the stolen thing," we know from this the nature of repentance for both positive and negative commandments — for they said that whoever is negligent, whether in positive commandments, or negative commandments, or in engaging with Torah, it is all as though he robbed the Shechinah from the arms of the Holy One, blessed be He. If so, repentance is always to restore the Shechinah to the Holy One, blessed be He, between His two arms — that is, with fear and with love, as will be explained further, that this is His own repentance, etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:25: However, the punishments differ according to the matter of the transgressions, whether positive or negative, as will be explained regarding the four categories of atonement — just as it is not equal in the matter of theft, for one may steal a penny and another may steal a hundred [coins] — so too it is not equal for one who steals the king's wife from between the king's arms to expose her outside his house, outside his palace, compared to one who exposes her among the nations of the world; and this is the matter of the repentance corresponding to weight — for one must weigh how great the blemish was, and suffer accordingly.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:26: One must further know, regarding the matter of repentance, that in all the places we explained in the Gate of Fear where sin causes blemish, in all of them repentance is needed.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:27: We explained in general that the blemish reaches into Atzilut, and reaches the inner Throne [Kise] through Israel's sins, blemishes the angels, blemishes the world — for the world's name is half meritorious and half guilty, and he tips the whole world to the scale of guilt — blemishes his own body, upon which the Torah has inscribed marks and all holy things, and the Shechinah departs from him, and likewise his holy soul departs from him, particularly regarding anger, as explained in parashat Tetzaveh (182b); and when the soul departs, the Shechinah too departs, for the soul is a part of her, as explained in the Tikkunim (Tikkun 62, 94b), in these words: and of that soul given to a person it is said (Genesis 1:27), "and God created man in His image" — in the pattern of the Shechinah. And it further says: whoever damages this pattern is as though he diminishes the Image, and the Shechinah does not rest there, and the secret of the matter is (Deuteronomy 31:17), "is it not because my God is not within me that these evils have found me" — the evils found me since the Shechinah has departed from me. — end of quotation. Here it is explicitly stated that when a person damages the pattern of his soul, he actually damages the Shechinah, from whom the image of the pattern of the soul was created, and the soul and the Shechinah, both together, depart from him, and then the outside forces rule over him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:28: The Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained in parashat Naso (Zohar 123a) that when the spirit of impurity rests upon a person, he is then called dead — this being "the wicked, in their lifetime, are called dead" — and he says there that the Shechinah, who is the final heh, is the breath by which man is sustained, in the manner of "for by every utterance of the mouth of the Lord does man live" (Deuteronomy 8:3), as we quoted in the Gate of Love, chapter 10, and he says, this heh does not depart from the body, and by it it is sustained; and when it departs from him, behold, the poison of death comes and rests upon him, which is called impurity, idolatry, invalidity, the angel of death, darkness and gloom, and it rests upon a person's body, and at that time the person is called dead — and the secret of the matter is (Ezekiel 18:32), "for I have no pleasure in the death of the dying, says the Lord God; therefore turn and live."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:29: They further say there, that just as there is a pattern of holiness, which is the Shechinah, from whom flows the abundance of holiness to man, to fulfill the 248 commandments which are her pattern, so there is an outside pattern that rests upon him to cause him to sin, and when a person sins, that evil pattern rests upon him, and according to his sin, so it clothes him. Therefore, when he first returns, he must strip off from himself this spirit of impurity and abandon it eternally, and it is good for him to enter a mikveh to strip off from himself this impurity — as they wrote in Sefer Chasidim — and we may infer to this the matter of the immersion of a convert: just as, in order to enter into holiness, if he did not immerse he has accomplished nothing, so is the matter for the wicked person who goes out — in order to enter into holiness, after he accepts upon himself not to return to his sin, he should immerse, and not be in the state of immersing while still holding an impure creeping thing in his hand.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:30: When one holds fast to repentance and its conditions, which we shall explain with God's help, he rectifies all the grades in which he caused blemish. So too they said (Zohar, parashat Naso 122b): Rabbi Yitzchak and Rabbi Yehudah were traveling from Usha to Lod. Rabbi Yehudah said, let us say words of Torah. "When a man opens a pit, or when a man digs a pit," etc. (Exodus 21:33) — what is written after it? "The owner of the pit shall pay." If this is so [for merely digging a pit], how much more so one who causes the world to be harmed through his sins! Rather, I am astonished — although he has harmed the world, why does he have repentance? Is it not written (Numbers 5:6), "a man or a woman who commits any sin that men commit," etc., "and shall confess their sin" and "restore"? Rather, surely this benefits them, because he performs repentance — so to speak, he actually rectifies it, for what he damaged above, he rectifies. And through what? Through repentance — and repentance rectifies everything: it rectifies above, it rectifies below, it rectifies himself, it rectifies the whole world. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:31: Now, according to Rabbi Yehudah's view, this "teshuvah" is the Supernal Mother, as is evident further on from Rabbi Yitzchak's words — and this repentance "rectifies above" — the blemish that is in Atzilut; "rectifies below" — the worlds from the Shechinah downward, the Throne and the angels; "rectifies himself" — the blemish within him that caused departure, in the manner of the story told in the Zohar (parashat Acharei Mot 75b), and likewise the soul that departed from him, and likewise the Shechinah, that she return to him, as it is said (Malachi 3:7), "return to Me, and I will return to you," and David the king, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 51:14), "restore to me the joy of Your salvation, and let a willing spirit sustain me."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:32: According to Rabbi Yitzchak's words, the repentance that every person performs is below — for not every person has the power to perform repentance so exalted that it ascends above, in the manner of David the king's repentance, peace be upon him — in these words: come and see, even the Assembly of Israel is called "teshuvah," and should you say that supernal repentance is not found everywhere — rather, this is called "teshuvah" when mercy turns back to receive her, and she returns over all the multitudes and nurses them; and complete repentance is when the soul surrenders to her and takes hold of her at the time she is in repentance, then everything is rectified above and below, and he and the whole world are rectified. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:33: Now, through the passages mentioned, we may understand what our sages, of blessed memory, said in Yoma (86a): great is repentance, for it reaches to the Throne of Glory, as it is said (Hosea 14:2), "return, O Israel, to the Lord your God." The meaning is that a person, according to the rank of his soul, causes a blemish in a corresponding grade — for if he has only a nefesh, his blemish is entirely in the aspects that are in Asiyah, where the Shechinah dwells in this world. And if he has a ru'ach, his blemish is higher, and if a neshamah, his blemish is in the Throne, whence souls are hewn, as explained above in the Tikkunim. And one who has a soul of Atzilut — no sin comes through him, as we quoted in the Gate of Fear. This is the merit of repentance — that it rectifies even if the blemish rose so far that it reached the Throne.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:34: Our sages, of blessed memory, said in the Midrash (Yalkut, Hosea, siman 532): Rabbi Yehudah bar Rabbi Simon said, "return, O Israel, to the Lord your God" — even if you denied the fundamental principle [of faith]. It is known (Kiddushin 40a) that the sin of idolatry, even in thought, causes blemish — unlike all other transgressions, as it is said (Ezekiel 14:5), "in order to grasp the house of Israel by their heart," whereas regarding other transgressions it is said (Psalms 66:18), "had I regarded iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have heard" — for thought is what causes blemish in the soul and in the Throne, and one thereby uproots himself from holiness and falls from the height of the firmament to the depth of the abyss, which is a strange god. And just as the blemish is through contemplation, so the rectification is through the contemplation of repentance — for repentant thoughts come from the side of the soul, and therefore our sages, of blessed memory, explained (Kiddushin 49b) that one who betroths a woman on condition that he is righteous, even if he was wicked, she is betrothed, since perhaps he had a thought of repentance. Here it is found that through his momentary contemplation, he ascended to the Throne of Glory to be called perfectly righteous — for from the Throne is the place where the souls of the righteous are hewn.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:35: Both these interpretations are revealed in the Midrash (Pesikta Rabbati, parashah 44), which says: our great teacher expounded, great is the power of repentance, for as soon as a person contemplates in his heart to repent, he immediately ascends and stands before the Throne of Glory — "return, O Israel, to the Lord your God" — the Holy One, blessed be He, says, even if there are transgressions in you "to the Lord" — up to the Throne of Glory — return, O Israel. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:36: It may also be reconciled in another manner: that complete repentance encompasses action, speech, and thought, which correspond to nefesh, ru'ach, and neshamah, as we explained in the Gate of Holiness, chapter 4. The reason is that when there is blemish in the nefesh, the ru'ach departs, because there is no throne for it to rest in; and once the ru'ach departs, the neshamah too departs to the Throne. It follows that the power of repentance must always ascend to the Throne in order to rectify Asiyah. Likewise, if he did not blemish through action but blemished through speech, then the ru'ach is blemished and the neshamah departs; if so, in returning, he must rectify the ru'ach and intend to draw down the neshamah. And likewise, if he blemished through thought, in the aspects we explained in Holiness, chapter 5, which is a blemish in the neshamah itself, in the very essence of the Throne, he must ascend to the Throne itself to rectify what he blemished there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:37: Further, on the aspects of repentance, it is explained in parashat Naso (Zohar 123a), of blessed memory: now we must return to the gate of repentance — for how many kinds of repentance do people perform, all of them good, but not all faces are equal. There is a person who is entirely wicked all his days, transgressing several negative commandments, who regrets and confesses them, and afterward does neither good nor evil — surely the Holy One, blessed be He, will forgive this one, but he will not merit the supernal repentance. There is a person who, after he returns from his sins and is atoned for, walks in the way of the commandments and engages with all his strength in fear and love of the Holy One, blessed be He — this one merits the lower repentance, called heh, and this is the lower repentance. And there is a person who, after regretting his sins and performing repentance, engages in Torah with fear and love of the Holy One, blessed be He, not in order to receive reward — this one merits the letter vav, which is the son of Yod-Heh, and by his name is called Binah, and this causes the vav to return [tashuv] to the heh. And the word "teshuvah" is thus: "tashuv vav le-heh" [the vav returns to the heh] — and never does the heh rest in a person, nor the yod, without the fear and love that are yod-heh. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:38: When you examine carefully the words of the Rashbi, peace be upon him, you will find in them the nature of repentance explained, in what appears to be a repetition of his language when he says, "there is a person who, after he returns from his sins, is atoned for" — what is the matter of "is atoned for," since he already said "returns from his sins" — surely he will be atoned for? Rather, this matter depends on the four categories of atonement that Rabbi Yishmael would expound (Yoma 86a) — that if he transgressed a negative commandment, he is not atoned for until Yom Kippur, for thus it says: if a person transgressed a negative commandment, repentance suspends and Yom Kippur atones; and if he transgressed [a sin punishable by] excision or death by the court, repentance and Yom Kippur suspend, and afflictions scour away [the sin]. It follows that he is atoned for only through afflictions. So too they said further on there, "there is a person who regrets his sins and performs repentance" — this too is a repetition, but it is in the manner explained: that one must perform repentance for each and every sin, and afflict himself with fasting and mortification — as we shall quote below the confessions of Rabbi Eleazar of Germiza [Worms], peace be upon him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:39: From this passage you further learn two things. First, that essential repentance is engaging in Torah with fear and love, through which one merits the supernal repentance — and of this we say in our prayer, "return us, our Father, to Your Torah" — for whoever is far from Torah is far from the Holy One, blessed be He, and "an ignorant person cannot fear sin, nor can an uneducated person be pious" — and therefore the essence of repentance is engaging in Torah, for the Torah teaches him how to return to appease his Creator and how not to stumble again. Second, that before he engages in Torah, he must first have regret and repentance — this being what it says, "after regretting his sins and performing repentance, he engages in Torah" — for before regret and repentance, his Torah is not desired and accepted, as it is said (Psalms 50:16), "but to the wicked, God says, what right have you to declare My statutes," and likewise, "any man who has a blemish shall not approach" (Leviticus 21:18) — and if this one reeks with the filth of his sins, how shall he draw near before the King? On the contrary, the King will draw away from him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:40: Regarding this, the pious Rabbi Yehudah bar Ila'i, peace be upon him, intended in saying (see Berachot 17a), "happy is he whose labor is in Torah and who brings contentment to his Maker" — meaning, one who engages in it clean of sin and guilt, so that the King delights in him and in his Torah. This was the merit of the early ones, whose Torah was so acceptable that they were even exempt from prayer (Shabbat 11a), because their Torah was clean. But one who is full of the stench of the filth of his sins, his Torah is not a contentment to his Creator. The reason is that through engaging in Torah, a person draws the Shechinah upon him, and when he is clean of sin, the Shechinah finds a throne and seat in which to sit and rest — like a person sitting on a properly fashioned chair, that chair is a contentment to him; so the Torah requires a clean, properly fashioned throne to draw the Shechinah to rest in it, but when a person is soiled with the stains of his sins, Torah does not rest in him, for there is no throne within him for either Torah or the Shechinah to rest, for every sin becomes a painful thorn and an irritating briar to one who sits on the throne. Therefore he must first wash away the filth of his sins through proper repentance, and afterward engage in Torah.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:41: He should take an example from the law of this matter established in the Gemara (Berachot 25a) and in the halachic authorities (Rambam, Laws of Shema 3:12; Tur, Orach Chaim 79), that in a place where there is a foul odor, it is forbidden to engage there in Torah and prayer, and one must distance four cubits from where the odor ends. So it is with one who engages in Torah while the impurity of the filth of his sins is upon him, for all the supernal holy ones distance themselves. It is likewise known that sins are called filth, as it is written (Isaiah 4:4), "if the Lord has washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion." And you find that Torah did not stand up for Doeg or Achitophel, for neither of them has a portion in the World to Come, even though they expounded several halachot as though from a tower flying in the air, as our sages, of blessed memory, explained in Chagigah (15b).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:42: The essence of Torah is repentance and action, and the punishment of a Torah scholar, if he sins, is greater than that of an ignorant person, as we learn in the chapter "Eilu Metziot" (Bava Metzia, end of ch. 2): Rabbi Yehudah bar Ila'i expounded, "and declare to My people their transgression," etc. — these are Torah scholars, for whom even unwitting errors are treated as intentional sins; "and to the house of Jacob their sin" — these are the ignorant common people, for whom intentional sins are treated as unwitting errors — and this is what we learn, Rabbi Yehudah says: be careful in your Talmudic study, for an error in study is accounted as intentional. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 2:43: Having explained the nature of repentance, let us explain its boundaries so that repentance be complete:
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:1: It is fitting to know that although we have said that the Holy One, blessed be He, receives the repentance of the penitent, the intent is not the abandonment of sin alone and regret alone, but rather one must weigh in his mind the matter of the transgression he committed — whether it is among those liable to negative commandments, or among those liable to excision and death by the court, or a desecration of the Divine Name — these being the four categories of atonement that Rabbi Yishmael would expound (Yoma 86a). We have already quoted his words in the Gate of Love, chapter 12, and in the Gate of Fear, the last chapter.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:2: Although Rabbi Yishmael said, if a person transgressed a positive commandment and performed repentance, he does not move from there until he is forgiven — one must still examine the weight of the commandment, which commandment was nullified. For we find that Reuben disturbed his father's bed, blemishing his father's honor, and prevented him (according to the view of the Kabbalists) from procreation — and there is support for this in the Zohar, parashat Vayishlach (176a); see there. And we find that he mortified himself with sackcloth and fasting, as they said in Bereishit Rabbah (84:19), in these words: "and Reuben returned to the pit" (Genesis 37:29) — and where had he been? Rabbi Eliezer says, engaged in his sackcloth and his fast; once he had finished, he went to the pit. The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: never has a person sinned before Me and performed repentance, and you have opened the way of repentance — by your life, your grandson shall stand and open with repentance — and who is this? Hosea, as it is said (Hosea 14:2), "return, O Israel, to the Lord your God." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:3: Should you say, but we already wrote above (ch. 1) that the first man and Cain opened the way of repentance — we may say that they opened repentance regarding a negative commandment, while Reuben's was regarding a positive commandment, as we explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:4: Further they said in the Sifrei (parashat Va'etchanan) on the verse "Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God," etc. — they said there, what Jacob our father, peace be upon him, said (Genesis 28:21), "and the Lord will be my God" — that His Name rest upon me, that no unfit thing come from me from beginning to end; and so it says (ibid. 35:22), "and it came to pass, while Israel dwelt in that land" — when Jacob heard [what followed], he trembled and said, perhaps some unfitness has occurred among my sons — until he was informed by the mouth of the Holy One, blessed be He, that Reuben had performed repentance, as it is said, "now the sons of Jacob were twelve" — did we not already know they were twelve? Rather, he was informed that Reuben had performed repentance — to teach you that Reuben would fast all his days, until Moses came and accepted him, as it is said (Deuteronomy 33:6), "let Reuben live and not die." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:5: Further, regarding the matter of David the king's repentance, peace be upon him, Scripture testifies of him (I Kings 15:5) that "nothing was found against him except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite" — and the meaning is that he killed him with the sword of the children of Ammon, as explained in the Zohar (parashat Mishpatim 107a) — for the matter of Bathsheba was entirely permitted, since every man who went out to David's wars would write a bill of divorce for his wife, as they elaborated at length in the Zohar (parashat Bereishit 8a-b).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:6: Our sages said (Avodah Zarah 4b), in these words: David was not fit for that act, as it is said (Psalms 109:22), "and my heart is wounded within me" — but rather, [it was allowed to happen] so that if an individual sins, they may say to him, behold, David sinned and the Holy One, blessed be He, accepted him [in repentance]. And so he himself said (Psalms 51:15), "I will teach transgressors Your ways, and sinners shall return to You" — as explained there in parashat Mishpatim on the page mentioned. And so they said in Midrash Tanchuma (Midrash Tehillim, mizmor 50): "many shall see and fear" (Psalms 40:4) — whoever wishes to repent should look to David; and so it says (Isaiah 55:4), "behold, I have made him a witness to the peoples" — immediately, "and shall trust in the Lord" (Psalms, ibid.). — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:7: Now, regarding the matter of David the king's repentance, peace be upon him, it is explained in the words of our sages, of blessed memory, and likewise in the Book of Psalms. Our sages, of blessed memory, said in Sanhedrin, chapter Chelek (107a): David was afflicted with tzara'at for six months, as it is said (Psalms 51:14), "restore to me the joy of Your salvation, and let a willing spirit sustain me." And from where do we derive these six months? As it is written (I Kings 2:11), "and the days that David reigned over Israel were forty years; in Hebron he reigned seven years, and in Jerusalem he reigned thirty-three years." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:8: Further, in Tanna Devei Eliyahu (Rabbah, ch. 2), regarding the matter of his repentance, on the verse (II Samuel 23:1), "now these are the last words of David" — in these words: another interpretation, "now these are the last words of David" — he said before Him, Master of the universe, just as You forgave my earlier sins, so forgive me for my later sins. Another interpretation: for twenty-two years the holy spirit departed from David king of Israel, and every single day he would shed a cup of tears and eat his bread with ashes, as it is said (Psalms 102:10), "for I have eaten ashes like bread." Another interpretation: he said before Him, Master of the universe, receive me in repentance, so that You may rebuke the wicked and say to them: if David king of Israel, who committed so severe a matter before Me, once he returned in repentance, I accepted him — how much more so would I accept you! And so he says (Psalms 51:6), "against You alone have I sinned," etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:9: Further, in Tanna Devei Eliyahu found among us in manuscript, in these words: "and King David was old, advanced in days, and they covered him with clothes" (I Kings 1:1) — this is what Scripture says (Isaiah 40:31), "but those who hope in the Lord shall renew their strength." Our sages, of blessed memory, said, for thirteen years David lay ill and bedridden, and seven mattresses would be changed under him every day because of the abundant discharge that flowed from his body — this being what is written (Psalms 6:7), "I drench my bed [with tears]" — these thirteen years of suffering were for the deed he did with Bathsheba, and all his enemies would say, when will he die? This being what Scripture says (ibid. 41:6), "my enemies speak evil of me: when will he die and his name perish?" And when he heard this, he gave his soul to prayer and supplications and sought mercy from before the Holy One, blessed be He, and said, Master of the worlds, sustain me for the sake of the Temple that Samuel the prophet handed to me, and please strengthen me and give me courage and raise me up and bring me down from this bed in peace, and let me complete for them my scroll — the building of the Temple. Immediately the Holy One, blessed be He, heard his prayer and he rose from his bed, as it is said (I Chronicles 28:2), "and King David rose to his feet" — and where else does a person stand if not on his feet? What is meant by "to his feet"? This teaches that he was healed and stood healthy. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:10: Further, a penitent must practice self-rebuke at least one hour a day, as we find David the king, peace be upon him, did; and so it is explained in the Zohar (parashat Mishpatim 107b), in these words: and it is written (II Samuel 15:30), "and David went up by the ascent of the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went up, with his head covered, and he walked barefoot." His head covered, and barefoot — why? Rather, he was rebuked, and he made himself rebuked to receive his punishment, and the people kept four cubits away from him. Happy is the servant who so serves his Master, that he recognizes his sin so as to return from it in complete repentance. Come and see, greater still was what Shimi son of Gera did to him, of all the distresses that passed over him until that day, and David did not respond to him at all a single word, for this was fitting for him, and through this his sins were atoned for. Now one must examine — Shimi was a Torah scholar and possessed great wisdom — why did he go out to David and do to him all that he did? Rather, the matter came from another place, and this matter was put into his heart, and all this was for David's benefit — for what Shimi did to him caused him to return in complete repentance, and it broke him with great breaking, and he poured forth many tears from within his heart before the Holy One, blessed be He; and therefore he said (II Samuel 16:10), "for the Lord has said to him, curse," knowing that this matter descended from a supernal place. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:11: From the totality of this passage, another lesson emerges for the penitent: that he must hear his own disgrace and not respond, in the manner of David. The reason is that the one insulting him is a messenger from above sent to insult him, and he must accept the judgment with a pleasant countenance. For behold, David did not actually possess those insults that Shimi son of Gera hurled at him, and yet he was silent and accepted them — how much more so one who sinned and transgressed greatly, in whom it is possible that everything said about him is true relative to the supernal blemish he caused.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:12: So too they further explained there (parashat Mishpatim 108, ad loc.) that the rectification of the Shechinah is a broken and contrite heart, and regarding the matter of sadness and bitterness — it "slaughters" the judgment, for the inclination overpowers a person's heart from the side of judgment, whose root is there, and when the heart is subdued, it indicates that judgment is subdued and bound beneath Chesed. Further, when a person sinned and would bring a sacrifice, it is through the attribute of mercy that his sacrifice is accepted — for by strict judgment, the sinning soul must die — but through the attribute of mercy, the Holy One, blessed be He, said, let him bring an animal soul in place of his own soul; and therefore regarding sacrifices it is not written "an offering to Elohim" but "to YHVH," which is mercy — and what is the sacrifice offered to Elohim? "A broken spirit" — for he actually sacrifices himself and his inclination in the breaking of his heart, bitterness, and sadness, as though he were dead — that same heart that grew strong in sin is now broken and dead. It follows that he actually offers the soul that dwells in the heart, and this is the sacrifice that Elohim desires. With this his words there are understood, in these words: "for You do not desire sacrifice, or I would give it" — does the Holy One, blessed be He, not desire that sacrifices be brought before Him? Surely He established, for the wicked, a sacrifice, that they bring it and their sins be atoned for — rather, David spoke before Elohim, and sacrifices are not brought to the name Elohim but to the name YHVH — for regarding harsh judgment, the attribute of judgment, sacrifices are not brought near, as it is written (Leviticus 1:2), "a man, when he brings from among you an offering to the Lord" — to the Lord [YHVH], and not to the name Elohim; and "when you bring a meal offering to the Lord," "a thanksgiving sacrifice to the Lord," "a peace offering to the Lord." Therefore, since David the king spoke to Elohim, it needed to be written (Psalms 51:18), "for You do not desire sacrifice, or I would give it; You do not delight in burnt offering" — for to this name, only "a broken spirit" is offered, as it is written, "the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit" — the sacrifice of Elohim is sadness and a broken heart. And therefore, whoever has a bad dream needs sadness and a broken spirit, and that sadness suffices for the bad dream, and judgment does not rule over him — for he has offered before Him the sacrifice fitting for the attribute of judgment. "A broken and contrite heart, O God, You will not despise" — what is "You will not despise"? This implies there is a heart that despises — this is not that heart which is proud, a heart with haughtiness of spirit; that is a heart that despises. But a broken and contrite heart, O God, You will not despise. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:13: Among the things the penitent must rectify is to rectify the sign of the covenant blemished through the emission of seed in vain, from which no person in our times is free in his youth. And they said in the Zohar that David was punished because he did not guard the sign of the covenant properly, in these words, in the Zohar (parashat Lech Lecha, end of p. 43): another passage opened and said, "though a camp encamp against me," etc. (Psalms 27:3) — so we have learned, "in this I trust" — what is "in this [be-zot]"? This is the sign of the covenant [ot brit] that is always ready with a person and is alluded to above, and therefore it is said "be-zot," as it is written (Genesis 9:12), "this [zot] is the sign of the covenant," "this [zot] is My covenant" (ibid. 17:10) — and all is at one grade. We have learned, "zeh" [this, masculine] and "zot" [this, feminine] are at one grade and are not separated. And should you say, if so, is not this the case for the rest of the people of the world? Why David alone and not another? Rather, because it is bound and alluded to in him, and it is the crown of Malchut. Come and see, because David the king did not guard this "zot" properly, kingship departed from him that entire time; and thus we have learned that this "zot" is alluded to in the supernal kingship and alluded to in Jerusalem, the holy city — at that moment David transgressed regarding it, a voice went out and said, in that by which you were bound, you shall be loosed — you shall be exiled from Jerusalem, and kingship shall depart from you — and so it was: in that by which a person transgresses, he is punished; and if David the king [was punished] thus, how much more so the rest of the people of the world! — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:14: Here it is explicitly stated that David received punishment because of the blemish of the covenant, and all his Torah and his deeds did not stand up to save him, and he was punished measure for measure, as explained in the passage. Likewise, every person should fittingly accept upon himself sufferings to purify what he blemished, and it is fitting that he go into exile, measure for measure, in the manner of David — as they said, exile atones for everything, in Sanhedrin (37b); see there. From this the discerning reader may infer regarding the other sins, that all of them require purification through suffering.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:15: In the Zohar (parashat Vayikra, end of p. 23), they further explained this matter regarding David's punishment, in these words: and should you say, David, who used to rise at midnight — why was judgment aroused against him? Rather, David was different, in that he transgressed regarding that to which he was bound, and required judgment, and in that he transgressed, he was judged — he sinned against the Holy Kingship and against Holy Jerusalem, and was driven from Jerusalem, and kingship departed from him, until he rectified himself properly and was punished. Rabbi Yehudah said, why did the Holy One, blessed be He, punish David through the agency of his son, as it is written (II Samuel 12:11), "behold, I will raise up evil against you from your own house"? Rabbi Yosi said, we have already established this — because if another person were to rise against him, he would not have mercy on him. He said to him, but did not Absalom seek to kill his father through several plots he devised against him? He said to him, I have not heard this; he said to him, I have heard this: David sinned with Bathsheba plainly, [and] the Holy One, blessed be He, said, let there come a son from the daughter of a strange god, and let him take his vengeance — and who is this? Absalom, who was the son of "the beautiful captive woman" [Ma'akah] taken in war. From this we learn that whoever takes a woman in war and desires her, in the end a wayward and rebellious son emerges from her — why? Because the impurity has not yet departed from her, as they have already established. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:16: As for saying that David sinned with Bathsheba plainly — the meaning is with the lower Bathsheba and the supernal Bathsheba, and the blemish of Bathsheba was that she ate unripe fruit — meaning that he benefited from the world without a blessing, as explained in the Zohar (parashat Tazria, end of p. 45), which we shall quote further on — and this is what Scripture testifies (II Samuel 12:12), "for you did it in secret," etc.
